'''Donald J. Summers''' (March 24, 1951 – March 3, 2021<ref>[https://www.colemanfuneralhome.com/obituaries/Donald-Summers-7/#!/Obituary Donald Summers]</ref>) was a particle physicist who worked on experiments at several labs, including [[Fermilab]], [[CERN]], [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]], and [[KEK]].

== Education ==
Summers received his undergraduate degree from the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]]. He completed his PhD from the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] in 1984, where his PhD advisor was Rollin John Morrison.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Donald J. Summers|url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/987154|url-status=live|access-date=March 12, 2021|website=INSPIRE-HEP|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210312144613/https://inspirehep.net/authors/987154 |archive-date=2021-03-12 }}</ref> While he was a graduate student, Summers worked on Fermilab's experiment E-516, a pioneering study of charmed particles, which are [[hadron]] particles containing one or more [[charm quark]]s. He helped with the design, construction, and reconstruction program for the experiment's SLIC (segmented liquid ionization [[Calorimeter (particle physics)|calorimeter]])<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Hoddeson|first1=Lillian|title=Fermilab : physics, the frontier, and megascience|last2=Kolb|first2=Adrienne|last3=Westfall|first3=Catherine|publisher=University of Chicago Press|year=2008|isbn=978-0-226-34623-6|location=Chicago|pages=276|oclc=192045754}}</ref> and assisted [[Michael Stewart Witherell|Michael Witherell]] with data analysis for this experiment.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bodnarczuk|first1=Mark|last2=Hoddeson|first2=Lillian|date=2008|title=Megascience in Particle Physics: The Birth of an Experiment String at Fermilab|url=https://online.ucpress.edu/hsns/article-abstract/38/4/508/105603/Megascience-in-Particle-Physics-The-Birth-of-an?redirectedFrom=fulltext|journal=Historical Studies in the Natural Sciences|volume=38|issue=4|pages=508–534|doi=10.1525/hsns.2008.38.4.508|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Career ==
After completing his PhD, Summers held a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral position]] with the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison|University of Wisconsin, Madison]] at CERN from 1984 to 1987, where he worked on [[UA1 experiment|UA1]],<ref name=":0" /> the experiment that had discovered the [[W and Z bosons]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=CERN-UA-001|url=https://inspirehep.net/experiments/1109643|url-status=live|access-date=March 12, 2021|website=INSPIRE-HEP|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210215034406/https://inspirehep.net/experiments/1109643 |archive-date=2021-02-15 }}</ref> He held another postdoctoral position at Fermilab from 1987 to 1989. He was a professor{{clarify|date=April 2021}} at the [[University of Mississippi]] from 1989 until his death in 2021.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Donald Summers - View Obituary & Service Information|url=https://www.colemanfuneralhome.com/obituaries/Donald-Summers-7/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210312220715/https://www.colemanfuneralhome.com/obituaries/Donald-Summers-7/|archive-date=March 12, 2021|access-date=2021-03-12|website=Donald Summers Obituary|language=en}}</ref> During this time, he also worked on the [[Compact Muon Solenoid|Compact Muon Solenoid Experiment]] at CERN, the [[BaBar experiment|BaBar Experiment]] at SLAC, the [[Belle II experiment|Belle II Experiment]] at KEK, and the [[Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment]] at Fermilab, among others.<ref name=":0" />
